## A Brief Defense of Getting Lost

There is a particular kind of knowledge that belongs only to people who have taken a wrong turn.

You know the route home, but not this staircase. You know the time, but not the name of the flower climbing the wall beside it. You have missed the bus, and for twenty minutes the day has opened a small door through which possibility slips.

Maps are wonderful inventions. They turn the world into a reassuring arrangement of lines, and they promise that if we pay enough attention, we will not be surprised. But perhaps we are meant to be surprised now and then. Perhaps efficiency is not the same thing as richness, and knowing exactly how to get from one place to another may reveal less about either than being gently, harmlessly lost.

Getting lost does not have to mean disaster. I am not proposing a hike into the wilderness without water or a romantic celebration of confusion. I mean the luxurious kind of getting lost: a safe neighborhood, a little daylight, a charged phone, and enough curiosity to regard the wrong street as an invitation rather than an accusation.

The body is a slow instrument. When we follow a route, we become efficient machines, anticipating corners and traffic lights. When we miss our turn, our senses come rushing back. We notice the warm stone of a building. The uneven rhythm of laundry being beaten on a balcony. A bicycle chained to a railing, its front basket full of lemons. Someone practicing the same four bars of music behind an upstairs window.

None of this was on the map.

The map said *residential area*. It did not say that a man on the ground floor was repairing chairs with bright blue thread, or that a cat sat on the windowsill as if waiting for a small ceremony, or that through a half-open door came the scent of cinnamon and woodsmoke.

We underestimate how much can happen in the space between certainty and arrival. We underestimate the mind that, given no clear instruction, suddenly begins to notice. We underestimate the stranger who appears because we turned left instead of right.

There is also something liberating about not knowing what comes next. Routine is comforting, but it can become a kind of invisibility. We repeat the same walk, see the same shops, inhabit the same familiar coordinates, and years pass while the world changes just outside the edge of our attention.

To get lost is to let the edges soften.

Not to abandon judgment, not to reject planning, and certainly not to confuse recklessness with freedom. But to recognize that not every minute needs a purpose. That curiosity is a form of respect. That the wrong turn may contain a view no efficient route could offer.

Sometimes the most important discovery is the place you meant to go. Sometimes it is the chair mender, or the lemons, or the song behind the window. Sometimes it is simply the knowledge that you are still capable of surprise.

And sometimes, on an ordinary afternoon, you arrive home a little later than expected, carrying nothing useful at all, except the sense that the world is larger—and more的具体, more tender, more alive—than the route you thought you knew.

"The Archive of Almost"

In a narrow building between a locksmith and a bakery that only opens on alternate Tuesdays, there was an archive of things that nearly happened.

No maps led... etc.
